questions.q: How many AU is one light-day?
questions.do: Look at the dashed red line on the One light-day chart and read its label.
questions.a: 173.14 AU. Light travels about 173 times the Earth–Sun distance in one day.

questions.q: When Voyager 1 is exactly one light-day away, how long after you send a message could its reply reach you? Does the page’s now answer match?
questions.do: Press Send Voyager 1 a message now and compare the two times it shows: when the message arrives and when the reply could reach you.
questions.a: 2 days: one day for the message to get there and one day for the reply to come back (signal time = distance ÷ speed of light). The page uses Voyager’s distance today, so its answer is close to 2 days around late 2026 and grows by about 3.6 AU of travel (about half an hour more each way) every year.

questions.q: How long would Voyager 2 take to cover the distance to the star Ross 248, and why is the published figure much shorter?
questions.do: Read the last line of the To the stars box.
questions.a: At 15.341 km/s, covering Ross 248's present 10.3 light-years takes about 201,000 years. The published figure is about 42,000 years because the star is moving towards us.

questions.q: Voyager 1 flies steadily away from the Sun. So why does its distance from Earth cross the one-light-day line, slip back under it, and cross again?
questions.do: Study the gold curve on the One light-day chart and read the note and the message below it.
questions.a: Voyager moves away at a steady 3.6 AU a year, but Earth circles the Sun, sometimes towards Voyager and sometimes away. That adds a wobble of up to 2 AU a year, so the distance rises in waves and crosses the line more than once.

questions.q: Both Voyagers were launched in 1977. When and at what distance from the Sun did each one cross into interstellar space?
questions.do: Read the footer at the bottom of the page (the sources list).
questions.a: Voyager 1: 25 August 2012 at 121 AU. Voyager 2: 5 November 2018 at 119.7 AU. Voyager 1 crossed about six years earlier, at nearly the same distance.
